stem: The 'era of one-party dominance' in Indian politics refers to the period when __________.
options: The Indian National Congress dominated elections and government (winning repeatedly), while other parties existed and competed freely
There was only one legally allowed party (a one-party state like the USSR)
solution: The 'era of one-party dominance' refers to the early decades after independence when the INDIAN NATIONAL CONGRESS DOMINATED Indian politics — winning election after election and forming governments at the centre and in most states. Crucially, this dominance occurred WITHIN a DEMOCRATIC framework: other parties existed and COMPETED FREELY in regular, fair elections; India was NOT a one-party state (like the USSR or China) where only one party is legally allowed. The Congress simply kept winning in a competitive multi-party system. So it means Congress dominance within a free, competitive democracy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's one-party dominance is different from one-party systems in other countries (like China or the former USSR) because __________.
options: In India, dominance was achieved democratically through free and fair multi-party elections (with opposition parties allowed and competing), whereas in one-party states only one party is legally permitted
In India there were no other parties
solution: India's one-party DOMINANCE is fundamentally DIFFERENT from the one-party SYSTEMS of countries like China or the former USSR. In India, the Congress's dominance was achieved DEMOCRATICALLY — through FREE and FAIR, competitive MULTI-PARTY ELECTIONS, in which OPPOSITION parties were fully ALLOWED to exist, organise, and compete. The Congress won because it secured the most votes/seats, not because rivals were banned. By contrast, in a true one-party STATE, only ONE party is LEGALLY PERMITTED and opposition is suppressed. This distinction — dominance won through open competition versus imposed monopoly — is crucial. So India's dominance was democratic and competitive, unlike coercive one-party states. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The first three general elections in India (1952, 1957, 1962) were all won convincingly by __________.
solution: The first three general elections in independent India — held in 1952, 1957, and 1962 — were all WON CONVINCINGLY by the INDIAN NATIONAL CONGRESS, which secured large majorities in the Lok Sabha and formed the government at the centre (under Jawaharlal Nehru), as well as governing most states. This repeated, comprehensive electoral success established the 'era of Congress dominance'. So the Congress won the first three general elections. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Election Commission of India, which conducts elections, is headed by the __________.
solution: The ELECTION COMMISSION of India — the independent constitutional body responsible for conducting and supervising elections — is headed by the CHIEF ELECTION COMMISSIONER (CEC). The Election Commission's task of organising India's massive elections (with a huge electorate, much of it illiterate, spread across a vast country) was itself an enormous undertaking, and its successful, impartial conduct of free and fair elections has been vital to Indian democracy. The first Chief Election Commissioner was Sukumar Sen. So the Election Commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The reasons for the Congress's early dominance included __________.
options: Its legacy as the party that led the freedom struggle, its wide social base and inclusive character, its strong organisation, and its towering leaders (like Nehru)
The banning of all other parties
solution: The Congress's early DOMINANCE stemmed from several genuine strengths: its LEGACY and PRESTIGE as the party that had LED the FREEDOM STRUGGLE (giving it enormous credibility and goodwill); its WIDE SOCIAL BASE and INCLUSIVE, 'umbrella' character (accommodating diverse groups, regions, castes, religions, and ideologies within it); its STRONG, well-spread ORGANISATION reaching down to the grassroots; and its TOWERING, popular LEADERS (above all Jawaharlal NEHRU, and others like Patel). These advantages, not any suppression of rivals, explain its repeated electoral victories. So the reasons included its freedom-struggle legacy, wide base, organisation, and leaders. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Congress is often described as an 'umbrella party' or a broad social/ideological coalition because __________.
options: It accommodated a wide range of groups, interests, regions, castes, religions, and ideological viewpoints within a single 'big tent'
It excluded everyone except one small group
It was a narrow single-issue party
solution: The Congress is described as an 'UMBRELLA PARTY' (or a broad coalition) because it ACCOMMODATED a WIDE RANGE of GROUPS, INTERESTS, REGIONS, CASTES, RELIGIONS, and IDEOLOGICAL VIEWPOINTS within a single 'BIG TENT'. During the freedom movement it had welcomed people of many persuasions — from the left to the right, and from various communities and classes — all united in the anti-colonial cause. After independence, it retained this inclusive, catch-all character, absorbing diverse elements and factions. This broad, accommodating nature was a key source of its wide appeal and dominance. So the Congress was an umbrella party accommodating diverse groups. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Within the Congress, there existed different factions and interest groups. This internal diversity functioned as __________.
options: A kind of 'system of factions' that provided internal checks, absorbed dissent, and even performed some functions of an opposition within the party
A reason it could never make decisions
A sign that it was a one-issue party
solution: Within the Congress there existed different FACTIONS and INTEREST GROUPS (based on region, ideology, personality, or interest). This internal DIVERSITY functioned as a kind of 'SYSTEM of FACTIONS' that gave the party remarkable flexibility: the factions competed and bargained WITHIN the party, providing internal CHECKS and balances, ABSORBING DISSENT and accommodating varied demands, and even performing some of the FUNCTIONS of an OPPOSITION (voicing criticism and alternative views) from INSIDE the ruling party. This helped the Congress remain broad-based and responsive, and contributed to its dominance. So the factions provided internal checks and an opposition-like role within the party. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Although the Congress dominated, there were opposition parties that played an important role. Which of the following was an opposition party of this era?
options: The Socialist parties, the Communist Party of India (CPI), the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, and the Swatantra Party
The Muslim League ruled the opposition alone
solution: Although the Congress dominated, several OPPOSITION PARTIES existed and played an important role in this era. These included: the SOCIALIST parties (e.g., the Praja Socialist Party, and socialists led by figures like Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia); the COMMUNIST PARTY of India (CPI); the BHARATIYA JANA SANGH (a right-wing, Hindu-nationalist party, forerunner of the BJP, associated with Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Deen Dayal Upadhyaya); and the SWATANTRA PARTY (a pro-free-market, right-of-centre party led by C. Rajagopalachari). These parties provided criticism, alternatives, and democratic competition. So opposition parties included the Socialists, CPI, Jana Sangh, and Swatantra Party. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The opposition parties, though small, were significant because they __________.
options: Kept the democratic spirit alive — offering criticism, principled alternatives, and a check on the ruling party, and maintaining a vibrant, competitive democracy
Were banned and had no role
solution: The OPPOSITION parties of this era, though SMALL in terms of seats, were significant because they KEPT the DEMOCRATIC SPIRIT ALIVE. They offered CRITICISM of government policies, put forward PRINCIPLED ALTERNATIVES and different ideological visions (socialist, communist, free-market, Hindu-nationalist), provided a CHECK on the dominant ruling party, produced many talented leaders, and maintained a VIBRANT, COMPETITIVE democracy. Their presence ensured that India's one-party dominance remained genuinely democratic (with real debate and choice) rather than becoming an authoritarian monopoly. So the opposition kept democracy vibrant and provided a check. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The first Communist government to be democratically elected in India (and one of the first anywhere in the world) came to power in __________.
solution: The first COMMUNIST government to be DEMOCRATICALLY ELECTED in India — and one of the first elected communist governments anywhere in the world — came to power in KERALA in 1957, led by E.M.S. NAMBOODIRIPAD (of the Communist Party of India). This was a landmark event, showing that even in the era of Congress dominance, opposition parties could win power at the state level through the ballot box. (This government was, however, later dismissed by the central government in 1959.) So the first elected communist government was in Kerala (1957). This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Swatantra Party, founded in 1959, is notable for advocating __________.
options: A free-market economy and limited state intervention (opposing the Congress's socialist-leaning, state-planned economic policies)
solution: The SWATANTRA PARTY, founded in 1959 (led by figures like C. Rajagopalachari, Minoo Masani, and N.G. Ranga), is notable for advocating a FREE-MARKET ECONOMY and LIMITED STATE INTERVENTION. It OPPOSED the Congress government's SOCIALIST-LEANING policies — such as extensive state PLANNING, nationalisation, heavy state control of the economy, and land ceilings — arguing instead for private enterprise, free trade, and less government control. It was a right-of-centre, pro-market party, distinctive in the Indian political spectrum of the time. So the Swatantra Party advocated a free-market economy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh (founded 1951) is significant as the forerunner/predecessor of which present-day party?
solution: The BHARATIYA JANA SANGH (founded in 1951, associated with Syama Prasad Mookerjee and, ideologically, with Deen Dayal Upadhyaya and the RSS) is significant as the FORERUNNER/predecessor of the present-day BHARATIYA JANATA PARTY (BJP). The Jana Sangh was a right-wing, Hindu-nationalist party; it later merged into the Janata Party (1977), and after that broke away to form the BJP in 1980. So the Jana Sangh was the forerunner of the BJP. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): India's early period is called an era of one-party dominance, not a one-party system. Reason (R): The Congress won repeatedly in free and fair elections in which opposition parties were allowed to compete, rather than dominance being imposed by banning rivals. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India's early period is called an era of one-party DOMINANCE, NOT a one-party SYSTEM. And the reason is (R) that the Congress won REPEATEDLY in FREE and FAIR ELECTIONS in which OPPOSITION parties were fully ALLOWED to exist and COMPETE — its dominance was EARNED through democratic competition, NOT IMPOSED by banning or suppressing rivals (as in a genuine one-party state). This democratic, competitive basis of Congress dominance is precisely why it is termed 'dominance' rather than a 'one-party system' (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Congress was able to accommodate diverse and even conflicting interests. Reason (R): As a broad umbrella party formed during the inclusive freedom struggle, it contained many factions and ideological tendencies within it. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Congress was able to ACCOMMODATE DIVERSE and even CONFLICTING interests. And the reason is (R) that, as a broad UMBRELLA party forged during the INCLUSIVE FREEDOM STRUGGLE (which had united people of many views against colonial rule), it CONTAINED many FACTIONS and IDEOLOGICAL TENDENCIES WITHIN it — from left to right, and across regions, castes, and communities. This internally diverse, coalition-like character is precisely what enabled the party to absorb and balance a wide array of interests (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The nature of the Congress as a broad coalition meant that its dominance was based partly on __________.
options: Its ability to bring together and represent very different social groups and interests, giving it wide appeal across the country
Appealing to only one narrow group
solution: The nature of the Congress as a BROAD COALITION meant that its dominance was based partly on its ABILITY to BRING TOGETHER and REPRESENT very DIFFERENT SOCIAL GROUPS and interests — high castes and low castes, rich and poor, various religions and communities, and different regions — within a single party. By accommodating and appealing to such a wide cross-section of Indian society, the Congress achieved WIDE APPEAL across the whole country, which translated into its broad electoral support and dominance. So its dominance rested partly on its capacity to unite and represent diverse groups. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The system of Congress dominance is sometimes called the '__________' after a political scientist's description.
options: 'Congress System' (a term associated with Rajni Kothari)
solution: The system of Congress dominance is sometimes called the 'CONGRESS SYSTEM' — a term associated with the political scientist Rajni KOTHARI. He described how the Congress functioned as a dominant party at the centre of the political system, with the opposition parties operating at the margins but exerting influence (partly through the Congress's own internal factions, which reflected different ideological pressures). The 'Congress System' captured this distinctive pattern of one-party dominance within a competitive democracy. So the term is the 'Congress System'. This is a prelims-relevant concept.

stem: The socialist leaders and parties in this era advocated __________.
options: Democratic socialism — greater economic equality, workers' and peasants' interests, and social justice, within a democratic framework
A free-market economy with no state role
solution: The SOCIALIST leaders and parties in this era (such as the Socialist Party and the Praja Socialist Party, with leaders like Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, and Acharya Narendra Dev) advocated DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISM — greater economic EQUALITY, the interests of WORKERS and PEASANTS, land reforms, and SOCIAL JUSTICE — to be achieved WITHIN a DEMOCRATIC framework (rejecting the authoritarian methods of communism). They often criticised the Congress for not being radical enough in implementing socialism and reducing inequality. So the socialists advocated democratic socialism and social justice. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches an opposition party with its ideological orientation?
options: CPI — communist/left; Socialist parties — democratic socialist; Swatantra Party — free-market/right; Jana Sangh — Hindu-nationalist/right
CPI — free-market; Swatantra — communist; Jana Sangh — socialist
Swatantra — Hindu nationalist; Jana Sangh — communist
solution: The correct matching of opposition parties with their ideological orientations is: the COMMUNIST PARTY of INDIA (CPI) — COMMUNIST/LEFT (advocating the interests of workers/peasants and, ultimately, socialism/communism); the SOCIALIST parties — DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST (equality and social justice within democracy); the SWATANTRA PARTY — FREE-MARKET/RIGHT (private enterprise, limited government); and the BHARATIYA JANA SANGH — HINDU-NATIONALIST/RIGHT (cultural nationalism, forerunner of the BJP). Knowing the ideological positions of these parties is prelims-relevant. So option 1 gives the correct matches. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 1967 general elections marked a turning point because __________.
options: The Congress's dominance was seriously challenged — it lost power in several states (to opposition coalitions) and its majority at the centre was reduced, signalling the decline of one-party dominance
The Congress won every single seat
solution: The 1967 general elections marked an important TURNING POINT in the era of Congress dominance. In these elections, the Congress's dominance was SERIOUSLY CHALLENGED for the first time: it LOST POWER in SEVERAL STATES (where opposition parties formed coalition governments — often called 'Samyukta Vidhayak Dal' or united legislature-party coalitions), and its MAJORITY at the CENTRE was significantly REDUCED (though it still formed the government). This signalled the beginning of the DECLINE of one-party dominance and the rise of a more competitive, coalitional politics. So 1967 marked the serious challenge to Congress dominance. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The first general election in India (1951–52) was a massive exercise because __________.
options: It involved a huge electorate of over 170 million voters, most of them illiterate and poor, spread across a vast country — an unprecedented democratic undertaking
Only a few thousand people voted
It was conducted by the British
solution: The first general election of 1951–52 was a MASSIVE and unprecedented exercise. It involved a HUGE ELECTORATE of over 170 million eligible voters — the MAJORITY of whom were ILLITERATE and POOR — spread across a VAST and diverse country with limited infrastructure. Conducting a free and fair election on this scale (with special measures like symbols for parties to help illiterate voters) was an enormous logistical and democratic achievement, watched with scepticism by many. Its success was a landmark for Indian democracy. So the first election was a massive exercise due to the enormous, largely illiterate electorate. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The first Chief Election Commissioner of India, who organised the first general elections, was __________.
solution: Sukumar SEN was the FIRST Chief Election Commissioner of India, and he had the monumental task of ORGANISING the FIRST GENERAL ELECTIONS (1951–52). He oversaw the preparation of electoral rolls for the enormous electorate, the design of the voting system (including party symbols for illiterate voters), the training of staff, and the logistics of polling across the country — successfully conducting a credible, free and fair election. So the first Chief Election Commissioner was Sukumar Sen. (T.N. Seshan was a later, well-known CEC.) This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: To help illiterate voters identify parties/candidates on the ballot, the Election Commission introduced __________.
options: Party symbols (distinctive election symbols for each party)
solution: To help the large number of ILLITERATE VOTERS identify parties and candidates on the ballot, the Election Commission introduced PARTY SYMBOLS — distinctive ELECTION SYMBOLS assigned to each party (and independent candidates) — so that voters who could not read could still recognise and vote for their chosen party by its symbol. This innovation was crucial for making universal adult franchise workable in a largely illiterate society, and party symbols remain a feature of Indian elections. So party symbols were introduced to help illiterate voters. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Communist Party of India (CPI) emerged as one of the significant opposition parties, drawing support especially from __________.
options: Workers, peasants, and certain regions (like parts of Kerala, West Bengal, and Andhra), advocating the interests of the working classes
solution: The COMMUNIST PARTY of INDIA (CPI) emerged as one of the significant OPPOSITION parties, drawing support especially from WORKERS (labour), PEASANTS, and certain REGIONS — such as parts of KERALA, WEST BENGAL, and ANDHRA (Telangana) — where it had a strong organisational and popular base. Ideologically committed to the interests of the WORKING CLASSES and the poor, the CPI championed land reforms, workers' rights, and radical social change. It became the main party of the parliamentary left in this era. So the CPI drew support from workers, peasants, and certain regions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The dismissal of the elected Communist government of Kerala in 1959 (by the central Congress government) illustrates __________.
options: A controversial early use of central power (President's Rule) against a state government of a rival party — raising debates about the misuse of such powers
That the Congress lost Kerala permanently
solution: The DISMISSAL of the democratically elected COMMUNIST government of KERALA in 1959 (by the central CONGRESS government, using the power to impose PRESIDENT'S RULE) illustrates a CONTROVERSIAL early use of CENTRAL POWER against a STATE government run by a RIVAL party. The central government cited law-and-order and agitation, but critics saw it as an unfair, politically motivated removal of a legitimately elected opposition government. This episode raised early and lasting DEBATES about the potential MISUSE of the central government's power to dismiss state governments — an issue of centre–state relations and federalism. So it illustrates a controversial use of central power against a rival state government. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The presence of a strong ruling party alongside a weaker but vocal opposition created a political system where __________.
options: The opposition, though unable to form a national government, influenced policy and public debate and held the ruling party accountable — sustaining meaningful democracy
The opposition had no influence whatsoever
There was no debate at all
The ruling party faced no scrutiny
solution: The presence of a strong ruling Congress alongside a weaker but VOCAL OPPOSITION created a political system in which the OPPOSITION — though unable (in this era) to form a national GOVERNMENT — nonetheless INFLUENCED POLICY and PUBLIC DEBATE, criticised and scrutinised the government, articulated alternative viewpoints, and thereby HELD the ruling party ACCOUNTABLE. This meaningful opposition (both in Parliament and through the Congress's own internal factions reflecting varied pressures) helped sustain a genuine, functioning DEMOCRACY, ensuring that dominance did not become unchecked domination. So the opposition influenced policy and held the ruling party accountable. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Leaders like Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia were associated with which political tendency?
solution: Jayaprakash NARAYAN (JP) and Ram Manohar LOHIA were leading figures of the SOCIALIST movement/parties in India. They advocated DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISM — social and economic equality, the interests of the poor and marginalised, and social justice — within a democratic framework, and often criticised the Congress from a socialist standpoint. (JP later became famous for leading the 'Total Revolution' movement against Indira Gandhi in the 1970s.) So JP and Lohia were associated with socialism. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh differed from the Congress especially in its emphasis on __________.
options: Cultural nationalism / a Hindu-nationalist vision (e.g., 'one country, one culture, one nation'), and issues like a strong unitary state and opposition to certain Congress policies
solution: The BHARATIYA JANA SANGH differed from the Congress especially in its emphasis on CULTURAL NATIONALISM and a HINDU-NATIONALIST vision. It promoted ideas like 'one country, one culture, one nation', favoured a strong, unitary Indian state, opposed the concept of appeasement of minorities as it saw it, advocated for Hindi and Indian cultural traditions, and took distinctive positions (e.g., on Kashmir, and against some Congress secular and economic policies). It was ideologically on the Hindu-nationalist right. So the Jana Sangh emphasised cultural/Hindu nationalism. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The internal factions of the Congress played a role similar to that of an opposition. Reason (R): Different ideological and interest groups within the party competed and voiced dissent, providing checks and reflecting diverse viewpoints inside the ruling party. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the INTERNAL FACTIONS of the Congress played a role SIMILAR to that of an OPPOSITION. And the reason is (R) that different IDEOLOGICAL and INTEREST GROUPS within the party COMPETED with one another, bargained, and VOICED DISSENT and criticism, thereby providing internal CHECKS and reflecting DIVERSE VIEWPOINTS INSIDE the ruling party. Because these factions performed the opposition-like functions of debate, criticism, and representation of varied interests within the Congress itself, they functioned much like an opposition (A). So R correctly explains A. This is a key feature of the 'Congress System'.

stem: Assertion (A): India's democracy remained vibrant even during the era of Congress dominance. Reason (R): Free and fair elections were held regularly, opposition parties functioned openly, and the press and civil liberties operated, keeping the system genuinely democratic. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India's DEMOCRACY remained VIBRANT even during the era of Congress dominance. And the reason is (R) that FREE and FAIR ELECTIONS were held REGULARLY, OPPOSITION parties FUNCTIONED OPENLY (competing, criticising, and sometimes winning power at the state level), and the PRESS and CIVIL LIBERTIES operated — keeping the system GENUINELY DEMOCRATIC and competitive. Because these democratic institutions and freedoms were maintained (and dominance was not imposed by force), the political system stayed vibrant despite one party's electoral predominance (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The socialist parties often criticised the Congress for __________.
options: Not doing enough to achieve genuine socialism and reduce inequality (being too moderate/gradual in its socialism)
solution: The SOCIALIST parties often CRITICISED the Congress for NOT doing ENOUGH to achieve GENUINE SOCIALISM and to REDUCE INEQUALITY. Although the Congress professed a 'socialistic pattern of society' and undertook planning and some reforms, the socialists argued it was too MODERATE, cautious, and GRADUAL — failing to implement radical land reforms, meaningfully redistribute wealth and power, or truly transform the lives of the poor, workers, and peasants. From the left, they pushed the Congress to be more genuinely egalitarian and pro-poor. So the socialists criticised the Congress for being too moderate in its socialism. So option 1 is correct.

stem: One reason India did not become a two-party or multi-party competitive system in its early decades was __________.
options: The Congress's overwhelming strength and broad appeal left little space for a single rival to match it, while the opposition remained fragmented across many small parties
The absence of any political parties
A law limiting parties to one
solution: One reason India did not become a competitive TWO-PARTY (or evenly balanced multi-party) system in its early decades was the CONGRESS's OVERWHELMING STRENGTH and BROAD, umbrella-like APPEAL, which left LITTLE SPACE for any SINGLE RIVAL party to match it across the whole country. Meanwhile, the OPPOSITION was FRAGMENTED across MANY SMALL parties of varied ideologies (communist, socialist, Hindu-nationalist, free-market, regional), which could not unite into a single strong alternative. This combination — a dominant, all-encompassing Congress facing a divided opposition — produced the pattern of one-party dominance. So the reason was Congress's strength plus a fragmented opposition. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The elections were contested and the results accepted peacefully, which shows that __________.
options: India's political parties and leaders accepted the democratic rules of the game — competing through elections and respecting the verdict — which was crucial to democracy's success
Only one party was allowed to contest
solution: The fact that elections were genuinely CONTESTED (by multiple parties) and the RESULTS ACCEPTED PEACEFULLY by winners and losers alike shows that India's political parties and leaders ACCEPTED the DEMOCRATIC RULES of the GAME — agreeing to COMPETE through the ballot box and to RESPECT the VERDICT of the voters (including transfers of power at the state level). This shared commitment to democratic norms and peaceful competition was CRUCIAL to the SUCCESS and consolidation of Indian democracy. So the peaceful acceptance of election results shows that parties accepted the democratic rules of the game. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE about the relationship between the Congress and the opposition in this era?
options: Many opposition leaders had themselves been part of the freedom struggle and shared a broad consensus on democracy and secularism, while differing on policy and ideology — so competition was mostly within agreed democratic limits
The opposition wanted to overthrow democracy
There was violent civil war between them
solution: It is TRUE that many OPPOSITION leaders had themselves been part of the FREEDOM STRUGGLE (as had the Congress), and shared with the Congress a BROAD CONSENSUS on the fundamentals — DEMOCRACY, SECULARISM, the Constitution, and national unity — while DIFFERING on POLICY and IDEOLOGY (economic direction, the pace of reform, cultural issues, etc.). As a result, political COMPETITION was largely conducted WITHIN agreed DEMOCRATIC LIMITS and shared national commitments, rather than as a struggle to destroy the system. This underlying consensus, amid genuine differences, helped Indian democracy function and endure. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The significance of studying the era of one-party dominance is that it shows __________.
options: How democracy took root and functioned in India — that dominance by one party can coexist with genuine democratic competition, and how the seeds of later multi-party politics were present
That India was always a two-party system
solution: The SIGNIFICANCE of studying the era of one-party dominance is that it shows HOW DEMOCRACY took ROOT and functioned in India in its formative decades. It demonstrates that DOMINANCE by ONE PARTY (the Congress) could COEXIST with GENUINE DEMOCRATIC COMPETITION — free elections, an active opposition, civil liberties, and internal party pluralism — rather than sliding into authoritarianism. It also reveals how the SEEDS of the later, more competitive MULTI-PARTY politics (the decline of Congress dominance and the rise of coalition politics) were already present in the opposition parties and the internal dynamics of the era. So studying it shows how democracy took root and how dominance coexisted with competition. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Praja Socialist Party (PSP) and other socialist parties suffered from __________, which weakened them as a challenge to the Congress.
options: Frequent splits, mergers, and internal divisions (organisational instability)
solution: The Praja Socialist Party (PSP) and other SOCIALIST parties suffered from FREQUENT SPLITS, MERGERS, and INTERNAL DIVISIONS — a pattern of organisational INSTABILITY and fragmentation (parties forming, breaking apart, and recombining). This chronic disunity and lack of a stable, cohesive organisation WEAKENED the socialists as an effective CHALLENGE to the Congress, preventing them from consolidating into a strong, united alternative. Organisational weakness was a recurring problem for much of the non-communist opposition. So the socialist parties were weakened by frequent splits and internal divisions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The dominance of the Congress at the national level was accompanied by __________ at the state level in the early years.
options: Congress governments in most states too (giving it power at both the centre and in the states)
solution: The DOMINANCE of the Congress at the NATIONAL (central) level was accompanied by CONGRESS GOVERNMENTS in MOST STATES as well, in the early years. Winning both the Lok Sabha elections and most state assembly elections, the Congress held power at BOTH the CENTRE and in the vast majority of the STATES. This dual dominance (centre and states) reinforced its overall predominance in the political system — though this too began to erode after 1967, when opposition parties captured several state governments. So Congress dominance extended to most states as well as the centre. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which statement best captures the paradox/distinctiveness of the 'Congress System'?
options: A single party dominated, yet democracy remained genuine and competitive — because opposition existed outside the party and diverse factions competed inside it
One party ruled by banning all others
solution: The PARADOX/distinctiveness of the 'CONGRESS SYSTEM' is best captured thus: a SINGLE PARTY (the Congress) DOMINATED the political landscape, YET DEMOCRACY remained GENUINE and COMPETITIVE. This was possible because meaningful OPPOSITION existed BOTH OUTSIDE the party (in the various opposition parties that competed freely) AND INSIDE it (in the diverse FACTIONS that competed and voiced dissent within the Congress itself). Thus dominance and democratic competition COEXISTED — an unusual and distinctive arrangement. So option 1 captures the paradox of the Congress System. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The decline of Congress dominance, beginning around 1967, eventually led to __________ in later decades.
options: A more competitive, multi-party and coalition politics (with regional parties and other national parties gaining power)
The permanent rule of the Congress
solution: The DECLINE of Congress dominance, beginning around 1967 (and unfolding over subsequent decades, with events like the Congress split, the Emergency, the 1977 Janata victory, and the later rise of regional and other national parties), eventually led to a MORE COMPETITIVE, MULTI-PARTY and COALITION POLITICS. In later decades, no single party could dominate as the Congress once had; REGIONAL PARTIES and other NATIONAL parties (like the Janata Party and later the BJP) gained power, and coalition governments became common. This transformation from one-party dominance to competitive coalition politics is a major theme of India's later political development. So the decline led to competitive multi-party/coalition politics. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In summary, the era of one-party dominance demonstrates that __________.
options: Indian democracy successfully established itself, with the Congress dominating through democratic means while a free opposition and competitive elections kept the system open and accountable
Elections were meaningless in this era
solution: In summary, the era of one-party dominance DEMONSTRATES that Indian DEMOCRACY SUCCESSFULLY ESTABLISHED itself in the crucial early decades. The CONGRESS DOMINATED, but it did so through DEMOCRATIC MEANS — winning free and fair elections on the strength of its legacy, broad appeal, organisation, and leadership — while a FREE OPPOSITION (of varied ideologies) and regular COMPETITIVE ELECTIONS, along with civil liberties and a free press, kept the political system OPEN, competitive, and ACCOUNTABLE. This shows that one-party dominance in India was compatible with, and even helped consolidate, a genuine and durable democracy. So the era demonstrates the successful establishment of Indian democracy through democratic dominance and a free opposition. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Swatantra Party opposed the Congress's policy of __________, arguing for private enterprise instead.
options: State control of the economy, nationalisation, and cooperative farming/land ceilings
solution: The SWATANTRA PARTY opposed the Congress government's policies of STATE CONTROL of the economy — including extensive state PLANNING, NATIONALISATION of industries and banks, licensing/permit controls, and measures like COOPERATIVE FARMING and LAND CEILINGS — arguing instead for PRIVATE ENTERPRISE, free markets, and minimal government interference. It championed economic freedom and the private sector against what it saw as excessive statism and 'socialistic' controls. So the Swatantra Party opposed state control/nationalisation and favoured private enterprise. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The system in which one party dominates but democracy remains competitive is best contrasted with __________.
options: A two-party system (like the USA/UK, where two major parties alternate in power) and a genuine one-party authoritarian system (like the former USSR)
A system identical to it in every way
solution: The Indian system of one-party DOMINANCE (within a competitive democracy) is best CONTRASTED with two other types: a TWO-PARTY SYSTEM — as in the USA or UK — where TWO major parties regularly ALTERNATE in power; and a genuine ONE-PARTY AUTHORITARIAN system — as in the former USSR or China — where only ONE party is legally allowed and there is no real competition. India's arrangement was distinct from both: a single dominant party, but with free competition and a real (if weaker) opposition. Understanding these contrasts clarifies what made the 'Congress System' distinctive. So it contrasts with two-party systems and one-party authoritarian systems. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The Congress accommodated diverse ideological currents within it. Reason (R): During the freedom movement, people with socialist, conservative, Gandhian, and other views all worked together in the Congress against colonial rule, and this pluralism carried over after independence. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Congress ACCOMMODATED DIVERSE IDEOLOGICAL currents within it. And the reason is (R) that during the FREEDOM MOVEMENT, people holding SOCIALIST, CONSERVATIVE, GANDHIAN, and other views all WORKED TOGETHER within the Congress in the common cause against COLONIAL rule, and this ingrained PLURALISM and habit of coexistence CARRIED OVER after independence. Because the party had always been an ideological 'big tent' forged in the unifying struggle, it continued to house varied tendencies afterward (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The peaceful transfer of power at the state level (e.g., to opposition governments) showed that __________.
options: The Congress and Indian democracy respected electoral verdicts even when the ruling party lost, a key sign of democratic maturity
The Congress refused to ever give up power
The military decided who governed states
solution: The PEACEFUL TRANSFER of power at the STATE level — for example, when opposition parties (like the Communists in Kerala in 1957, or the coalitions after 1967) won and formed governments — showed that the CONGRESS and Indian DEMOCRACY RESPECTED ELECTORAL VERDICTS EVEN when the ruling party LOST. Accepting defeat and allowing rivals to take office through the ballot box (rather than clinging to power by force) is a KEY SIGN of DEMOCRATIC MATURITY and the health of the system. So these peaceful transfers showed respect for electoral verdicts and democratic maturity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The role of regional and smaller parties in this era foreshadowed __________.
options: The later rise of powerful regional parties and coalition politics that would reshape Indian democracy in subsequent decades
The end of all regional identities
solution: The presence and role of REGIONAL and smaller parties in this era (such as early regional and state-based parties, and the diverse opposition) FORESHADOWED the LATER RISE of POWERFUL REGIONAL PARTIES and COALITION POLITICS that would RESHAPE Indian democracy in the following decades. As Congress dominance declined, regional parties grew stronger, captured state governments, and eventually became crucial players in national coalition governments — transforming India into a more federal, multi-party, and coalition-based democracy. The seeds of this were visible even during the era of dominance. So they foreshadowed the rise of regional parties and coalition politics. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following was a key strength of the Congress organisation in the early years?
options: A network of party units reaching down to the local/village level, connecting the party to people across the country
It existed only in one city
solution: A KEY STRENGTH of the Congress ORGANISATION in the early years was its extensive NETWORK of party units reaching DOWN to the LOCAL and VILLAGE LEVEL, built up over decades of the freedom struggle. This deep, countrywide organisation CONNECTED the party to PEOPLE across India, enabling it to mobilise support, communicate with voters, resolve local issues, and win elections at every level. This organisational depth and reach was a major advantage over the opposition parties, which were often organisationally weak. So a key strength was its grassroots organisational network. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The era of one-party dominance is best understood as a __________ of Indian democracy.
options: Formative/foundational phase (during which democratic institutions and practices took root)
solution: The era of one-party dominance is best understood as a FORMATIVE/FOUNDATIONAL PHASE of Indian democracy. During this period, the essential democratic INSTITUTIONS and PRACTICES — regular free and fair elections, an independent Election Commission, a functioning Parliament and state legislatures, an active (if weaker) opposition, civil liberties, and the peaceful acceptance of electoral verdicts — TOOK ROOT and were consolidated. This laid the durable foundations on which India's subsequent, more competitive democratic politics developed. So it was a formative/foundational phase of Indian democracy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter helps us understand that party systems can take different forms. Which of the following is a correct classification?
options: One-party (authoritarian) systems, two-party systems, multi-party systems, and one-party-dominant systems (like India's early years)
There is only one possible type of party system
solution: The chapter helps us understand that PARTY SYSTEMS can take DIFFERENT FORMS. A correct classification includes: ONE-PARTY (authoritarian) SYSTEMS (only one party legally allowed, as in the former USSR/China); TWO-PARTY SYSTEMS (two major parties alternate in power, as in the USA/UK); MULTI-PARTY SYSTEMS (many parties compete and often form coalitions); and ONE-PARTY-DOMINANT SYSTEMS (one party dominates within a competitive democracy — as in India's early years, and historically in a few other countries). Recognising these types clarifies where India's 'Congress System' fits. So option 1 gives a correct classification of party systems. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall lesson from India's early party system is that __________.
options: A dominant party need not undermine democracy if free competition, an active opposition, and democratic norms are maintained — dominance and democracy can coexist
Democracy requires the banning of dominant parties
solution: The overall LESSON from India's early party system is that a DOMINANT PARTY need NOT UNDERMINE DEMOCRACY — provided that FREE COMPETITION, an ACTIVE OPPOSITION, and DEMOCRATIC NORMS (free elections, civil liberties, respect for verdicts) are maintained. India's experience shows that DOMINANCE and DEMOCRACY can COEXIST: the Congress's predominance did not extinguish democratic competition or freedoms, because the system remained open and contestable. This is an important insight into how democracies can function even when one party is electorally preponderant. So the lesson is that dominance and democracy can coexist under democratic conditions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, the 'era of one-party dominance' shows that India __________.
options: Built a stable, functioning democracy in its early decades under Congress leadership, while nurturing the competitive, pluralistic politics that would follow
Failed as a democracy from the start
solution: In conclusion, the 'era of one-party dominance' shows that INDIA BUILT a STABLE, FUNCTIONING DEMOCRACY in its early decades under CONGRESS LEADERSHIP — establishing and consolidating democratic institutions, holding regular free elections, and governing a vast, diverse, poor country democratically — WHILE also NURTURING the COMPETITIVE, PLURALISTIC politics (an active opposition, internal party diversity, regional currents) that would FOLLOW as Congress dominance eventually declined. It thus represents both the successful founding of Indian democracy and the seedbed of its later, more competitive phase. So India built a stable democracy while nurturing the pluralistic politics to come. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Era of One-Party Dominance' is that:
options: India was a one-party dictatorship with no opposition

In the first few decades after independence, Indian politics was marked by the DOMINANCE of the Indian National Congress — which won the first three general elections (1952, 1957, 1962) and governed at the centre and in most states — but this dominance was achieved DEMOCRATICALLY through free and fair, competitive multi-party elections (unlike coercive one-party states), and rested on the Congress's freedom-struggle legacy, its character as a broad, inclusive 'umbrella' party with internal factions, its strong organisation, and its towering leaders; meanwhile, opposition parties (Socialists, CPI, Jana Sangh, Swatantra) existed and kept democracy vibrant and competitive (even winning power, e.g., the Communists in Kerala in 1957), and the Congress's dominance eventually began to decline (notably after 1967)
The Congress never won any election
solution: The chapter's overall message is that, in the first few decades after independence, Indian politics was marked by the DOMINANCE of the INDIAN NATIONAL CONGRESS. The Congress won the first three general ELECTIONS (1952, 1957, 1962) by large margins and governed both at the CENTRE (under Nehru) and in most STATES. Crucially, however, this was an era of one-party DOMINANCE, NOT a one-party SYSTEM: the Congress's dominance was achieved DEMOCRATICALLY, through FREE and FAIR, COMPETITIVE MULTI-PARTY elections in which OPPOSITION parties were fully allowed to exist and compete — unlike the coercive one-party states of the USSR or China. The Congress's dominance rested on genuine strengths: its LEGACY as the party of the FREEDOM STRUGGLE; its character as a broad, INCLUSIVE 'UMBRELLA' party that accommodated diverse groups and contained many internal FACTIONS (which provided internal checks and an opposition-like role); its strong, wide-reaching ORGANISATION; and its towering, popular LEADERS (above all Nehru). At the same time, a range of OPPOSITION parties — the SOCIALISTS, the COMMUNIST Party of India (which even won power in KERALA in 1957, one of the first elected communist governments in the world), the Hindu-nationalist JANA SANGH (forerunner of the BJP), and the pro-market SWATANTRA Party — existed and played a vital role, offering criticism, alternatives, and a democratic CHECK, and keeping Indian democracy VIBRANT and COMPETITIVE. This distinctive pattern (the 'Congress System') eventually began to DECLINE, notably after the 1967 elections, when the Congress lost power in several states and its central majority shrank. So the overall message is option 2.
